title: Site Conditions: Geology, Water, Climate

concepts.title: The water is already in your hole
concepts.mechanism: This island sits on porous limestone with groundwater near sea level — usually within a few feet of the surface everywhere near the coast. Dig a pit anywhere on site and it does not stay dry: water seeps in from the sides and bottom until it reaches the same level as the water table around it, like digging a hole on a beach. You are never 'keeping water out' of an excavation here — you are always managing water that is already inside it.
concepts.mechanismPro: Groundwater at ~sea level in a karst aquifer; expect seepage in any excavation below the water table, plan sump pumps or wellpoints, and remember the rock's porosity means pumped water recharges fast — you cannot dewater it away, only manage the inflow.
concepts.hook: Dig a hole on the beach at low tide — it fills with water anyway, from underneath, no matter how fast you scoop. The whole island is that beach.

applied.prompt: A foundation pit for a coastal structure is designed assuming dry excavation, no dewatering budget. Geotech flags groundwater at 4 ft. Your call?

options.label: Add a dewatering line item (sumps/wellpoints) and re-sequence around it now
options.outcome: Right. Budgeting for the water that is already there, before you dig, is far cheaper than a stalled excavation discovering it live.

options.label: Start digging and see how bad it actually is
options.outcome: You lose days re-mobilizing pumps mid-excavation, and the schedule float built for other risks gets spent on this one instead.

options.label: Trust the original dry-excavation assumption
options.outcome: The pit floods on schedule, exactly as the geotech report predicted. This is the same hydrostatic-uplift world as an empty pool — ignoring the water table never makes it go away.

applied.debrief: This is the base fact every later decision sits on: rock, water, and weather. The same water table that floods a pit here is what makes an empty pool float in V3-3 — one law, showing up everywhere you dig or build hollow on this island.

concepts.title: The slab sits on a sandwich, not on sand
concepts.mechanism: With groundwater near sea level, every slab on this project floats just centimeters above wet ground. Concrete is porous, and that ground pushes moisture up into it two different ways: wicking (capillary action, climbing the pores) and invisible water vapor. So before the pour, you build a sandwich: coarse gravel first — gaps too big for capillary action to grip, the capillary break — then a poly sheet on top of that to stop the vapor the gravel can't touch. Skip either layer and the slab quietly becomes a wet ceiling for the ground below it. There is no fixing it later: once the concrete is poured, both layers are buried forever.
concepts.mechanismPro: Capillary break (coarse, clean gravel) plus a vapor retarder (poly sheet, ideally under a protective layer to avoid puncture during the pour) belong under every slab-on-grade here; skipping either invites lifetime moisture emission through the slab — flooring adhesive failure, mold under vinyl, and warranty claims that surface only after handover.
concepts.hook: A dry cracker left on a damp sponge overnight goes soft by morning — nothing dripped or flowed, the moisture just migrated. Rest the cracker on a wire rack (gravel) with cling film underneath (poly) instead, and it stays crisp.

applied.prompt: After a wet-season dewatering delay, the concrete sub proposes pouring the next block of house slabs directly on compacted fill to claw back schedule — 'the gravel and poly are a nice-to-have, the soil's compacted and drains fine.'

options.label: Hold one day per block to place gravel and poly properly before pouring
options.outcome: Right. The day lost is recoverable; the buried layer is not — this is the only point in the entire life of the house these layers can ever be installed.

options.label: Pour with poly only, skipping the gravel layer
options.outcome: Handles the vapor, but poly laid directly on sharp compacted fill punctures easily during the pour, and without the gravel break beneath it you've lost the wick-stopping function entirely.

options.label: Pour directly on compacted fill to hold schedule
options.outcome: Compaction controls settlement, not capillary rise or vapor — every house poured this way gets a lifetime moisture path straight up through its slab, discovered only when flooring starts failing after handover.

applied.debrief: Same law, new disguise as S4's rising damp: there the wick climbs a wall, here it climbs through a floor — turn that wall diagram 90 degrees and it's this one. The poly layer is also your first brush with the invisible mechanism V3-5 explains in full: vapor, not just liquid water, is trying to get in.

summary: Everything on this project sits on young carbonate limestone with groundwater near sea level and a six-month hurricane season. This module teaches the physics of the site — rock, water, and weather — because every later decision (excavation pricing, canal methods, schedule windows, structural design) is downstream of these three facts.

sections.heading: The rock: limestone, not soil
sections.body: New Providence is carbonate rock: young oolitic/eolianite limestone over the older Lucayan Limestone. There is effectively no soil — vegetation sits on inches of organics over rock. Practical consequences: (1) all excavation is ROCK excavation — hydraulic breakers, rippers, and in heavy cuts drill-and-blast; (2) blasting near the occupied subdivisions on both flanks of the site triggers vibration monitoring, pre-blast surveys of neighboring homes, and community relations work; (3) the rock is KARSTIC — voids, caves and soft pockets appear randomly, so you run geotechnical borings on a grid and carry contingency for void grouting under building pads; (4) excavated limestone is an ASSET — it crushes into road base and fill. Cut-to-fill mass balance is one of the largest single cost levers on the whole project: canal, marina, and lake excavation should be balanced against fill needs before a single truck is hired.

sections.heading: The water: a lens at sea level
sections.body: The freshwater lens sits under 1.5 m below grade in places; near the coast, groundwater is essentially at sea level. Canals, the marina, and the three lakes all cut BELOW the water table — canal excavation happens 'in the wet' or behind temporary rock plugs that are cut last. The lakes will intersect groundwater and behave as groundwater windows: expect brackish, tidal-damped water, and design them as stormwater/amenity hybrids, never as freshwater ponds. You cannot hold a lake at a level different from the water table. Stormwater on New Providence goes to ground via drainage wells and soakaways cut into the porous rock — not to storm sewer outfalls. The drainage design is wells, swales, and the lakes.

sections.heading: The weather: schedule geometry
sections.body: Hurricane season runs June 1 – November 30, peaking mid-August through October. Rainy season is roughly May–October (~1,250 mm/yr). Rules the project must live by: marine works (dredging, groins, beach fill) are planned for the calmer late-fall-to-spring window; nothing weather-vulnerable (open shoreline excavations, half-built roofs, staged sand) is exposed through peak season without a written hurricane preparedness plan per contractor — tie-down procedures, demobilization triggers at 72/48/24 hours, crane laydown rules. Every contract needs a named-storm force majeure clause with defined standby and remobilization cost treatment: this is one of the most commonly bungled clauses in Caribbean contracts.

sections.heading: Codes and loads
sections.body: The Bahamas Building Code has been compulsory since the 1970s — the Bahamas was early in the region on codified wind standards. Practice on New Providence commonly references Florida Building Code / ASCE 7 wind methodology. Design wind speeds are in the 150+ mph class; reinforced concrete block or poured concrete construction dominates; hurricane strapping, ring beams, and impact/shutter protection are standard. Coastal buildings — the beach club, condos 1–2, marina structures — add flood elevation and wave-load design on top.

quiz.teach: On New Providence, 'digging' means breaking rock. The upside is that the excavated limestone is valuable — it crushes into road base and structural fill.
quiz.prompt: Why should canal, marina, and lake excavation be planned against fill needs BEFORE hiring any trucking?

choices.text: Because cut-to-fill mass balance is one of the largest cost levers on the project — own spoil crushed on site replaces imported base and fill
choices.why: Correct. Every cubic yard you reuse avoids both a disposal haul AND an import purchase — a double saving.

choices.text: Because trucking companies require long-term contracts
choices.why: Trucking terms are negotiable; the real issue is that hauling spoil out while importing fill pays twice for the same material movement.

choices.text: Because the government requires a mass-balance report before permits
choices.why: No such report is required. The driver is pure economics: reuse of spoil as crushed base saves $25–45/cy versus importing.

choices.text: Because excavated limestone can't legally leave the site
choices.why: It can leave the site. The point is you don't WANT it to — it's your cheapest source of road base and fill.

quiz.explanation: The site's biggest excavations (canals, marina basin, lakes) produce rock, and its biggest fills (roads, building pads) consume rock. Balancing them on paper first — a mass-balance plan you direct-manage, never delegate to the earthworks sub — is one of the largest single cost levers on the project.

quiz.teach: Karst is limestone that groundwater has dissolved into voids, caves, and soft pockets — and they appear randomly, not where it's convenient.
quiz.prompt: What is the standard defense against karst surprises under building pads?

choices.text: Geotechnical borings on a grid, plus a contingency budget for void grouting
choices.why: Correct — you can't eliminate karst risk, so you characterize it statistically (grid borings) and price the response (grouting contingency).

choices.text: Deep pile foundations under every building
choices.why: Massive overkill — limestone bearing is superb where sound. You'd pay pile-foundation money on 400+ structures to solve a localized problem.

choices.text: Ground-penetrating radar of the entire site before purchase
choices.why: GPR helps but can't see deep voids reliably in wet carbonate rock; borings on a grid remain the standard, with contingency for what the grid misses.

choices.text: Avoiding excavation entirely
choices.why: Impossible here — canals, lakes, utilities, and pools all require cutting rock. The answer is characterization plus priced contingency, not avoidance.

quiz.explanation: You manage karst the way you manage any random-occurrence risk: sample it (boring grid), carry a priced response (void grouting contingency), and put rock-quantity risk into unit-rate contract structures so a surprise is a measured quantity, not a claim.

quiz.teach: The three lakes will cut below the water table into porous rock. That makes them 'groundwater windows' — openings that expose the actual groundwater surface.
quiz.prompt: The landscape architect's renders show the lakes held 2 ft above surrounding grade water levels, sparkling and fresh. What's wrong?

choices.text: You cannot hold a lake in porous limestone at a level different from the water table, and the water will be brackish, not fresh
choices.why: Correct on both counts — the rock is porous, so lake level = water table level, and near the coast that water is brackish and tidally damped.

choices.text: Nothing — a pond liner will hold the design level
choices.why: There is no liner debate here as in clay-country lakes: these are groundwater windows by design. A liner defeats their stormwater function and fights hydrostatic uplift forever.

choices.text: The lakes only need pumps to stay at the render level
choices.why: Pumping against porous rock is pouring money into the ground — inflow through the rock is continuous and unlimited.

choices.text: The render is fine as long as the lakes are shallow
choices.why: Shallow makes it worse: shallow tropical lakes become algae soup. Good practice keeps a significant portion deeper than 6–8 ft.

quiz.explanation: This is a real sim scenario from the knowledge base: renders showing lake levels above the water table. The CM's job is to catch this at design review — before it's sold to buyers — because physics will win. Lakes here are stormwater/amenity hybrids at water-table level, brackish, with depth and aeration managed for water quality.

quiz.teach: Hurricane preparedness plans work on countdown triggers before forecast landfall — each window has its own actions.
quiz.prompt: Put these hurricane-season events in the order they occur across a season and an approaching storm:
items: June 1 — hurricane season opens; every contractor's written preparedness plan must already be rehearsed
Mid-August — peak season begins; no weather-vulnerable work exposed without a plan
72 hours out — preparedness plan triggers first actions (secure materials, review tie-downs)
48 hours out — demobilization decisions; cranes laid down per plan
24 hours out — site secured and evacuated; standby cost treatment per the force majeure clause
quiz.explanation: The preparedness plan is written and rehearsed BEFORE June 1, then executes on 72/48/24-hour triggers when a named storm approaches. Who pays for standby and remobilization is decided by the force majeure clause you wrote at contract signing — not negotiated in the storm's cone.

quiz.teach: Blasting is the cheap way to cut heavy rock — but this site has occupied subdivisions on both flanks.
quiz.prompt: What does blasting next to existing neighborhoods trigger?

choices.text: Vibration monitoring, pre-blast condition surveys of neighboring homes, and a community relations program
choices.why: Correct — the pre-blast survey is your legal defense against damage claims, monitoring proves compliance, and community relations keeps complaints out of DEPP and the press.

choices.text: Nothing extra, as long as the blaster is licensed
choices.why: A licensed blaster is necessary but not sufficient. Without pre-blast surveys, every existing crack in every neighboring house becomes your crack.

choices.text: A ban — blasting near homes is prohibited in the Bahamas
choices.why: Not prohibited — it's managed. Blasting at volume runs $8–20/cy versus $15–40/cy for breakers, so managed blasting is often worth the overhead.

choices.text: Only a notification letter to neighbors
choices.why: A letter without a pre-blast survey leaves you defenseless against claims that your blasting caused pre-existing damage.

quiz.explanation: Pre-blast surveys document neighboring structures' condition BEFORE work, so damage claims can be judged against a baseline. Combined with vibration monitoring and proactive neighbor communication, this is what makes blasting politically and legally survivable next to occupied communities.

quiz.teach: Stormwater design here looks nothing like a mainland subdivision.
quiz.prompt: Where does stormwater go on New Providence?

choices.text: Into the ground — drainage wells and soakaways cut into the porous rock, plus swales and the lakes
choices.why: Correct. The porous limestone IS the drainage system; wells and soakaways feed it, and the lakes buffer it.

choices.text: Storm sewers to ocean outfalls
choices.why: There is no island storm-sewer-to-outfall system; the porous rock accepts the water directly through drainage wells.

choices.text: Retention ponds sized to hold the 100-year storm
choices.why: The lakes do play a stormwater role, but the primary mechanism is infiltration to ground through wells and soakaways — the rock is the pond.

choices.text: Pumped to the municipal wastewater plant
choices.why: There is no island-wide wastewater system at all — the development builds its own package plant, and stormwater never goes there anyway.

quiz.explanation: Drainage wells ($8,000–20,000 each) and soakaways put stormwater into the porous limestone. The three lakes double as stormwater management. This is why the civil drainage design gets reviewed by MOW's Civil Design Section as part of permitting.

quiz.teach: The water table doesn't just threaten open excavations — it threatens every slab poured above it, silently.
quiz.prompt: A house slab is poured directly on compacted fill, skipping the gravel layer and poly sheet, to save a day on a delayed schedule. What actually goes wrong?

choices.text: Groundwater wicks upward through the porous concrete and vapor migrates through it, moving moisture into the slab continuously for the life of the house
choices.why: Correct — this is capillary action plus vapor diffusion, neither of which cares that the fill is 'compacted and drains fine.' Compaction controls settlement, not moisture migration.

choices.text: Nothing, as long as the fill is well compacted and slopes away from the house
choices.why: Compaction and slope manage bulk surface water, not water climbing through the pores of the concrete itself — a different mechanism entirely.

choices.text: The slab will crack from differential settlement within a year
choices.why: That's V3-4's mechanism (uneven support), not this one — a uniformly compacted pad settles evenly; the problem here is moisture transport, not settlement.

choices.text: Only a concern if the house is directly above the water table, not centimeters above it
choices.why: With groundwater near sea level, 'centimeters above' is exactly the condition every slab here is built in — there is no safe distance that skips the capillary break.

quiz.explanation: This is the 'under-slab sandwich' every slab needs on this island: gravel breaks the capillary wick, poly stops the vapor the gravel can't. Skip either and the ground becomes a permanent, invisible moisture source feeding straight into flooring adhesive and finishes above.

mathVariables.label: Design wind speed class
mathVariables.note: Florida Building Code / ASCE 7 methodology commonly referenced

decisionPoints.title: The render vs. the water table
decisionPoints.scenario: Marketing is about to publish landscape renders showing the three lakes at a level roughly 2 ft above what your geotech report says the groundwater sits at, with captions calling them 'freshwater lakes.' The landscape architect says the levels are 'aspirational.' Sales loves the images.

options.label: Stop publication, brief sales and the landscape architect on groundwater-window physics, reissue renders at true water-table level as brackish amenity lakes
options.outcome: A week of friction with marketing and a redesign fee — versus buyers who were sold something physics cannot deliver. Renders reissue honestly; the lake edge design improves because it's now designed for the real water level.

options.label: Publish — buyers won't measure lake levels
options.outcome: Early buyers close on the imagery. Two years later the lakes sit exactly at the water table, brackish and 2 ft below the renders' edge treatment, which now stands exposed. The HOA-in-formation makes it their founding grievance, and every future marketing claim gets discounted.

options.label: Ask the civil engineer to design a lined, pumped lake to hold the render level
options.outcome: The engineer's memo explains what you should have known: liners in porous rock fight hydrostatic uplift permanently, and pumping against unlimited inflow through porous limestone is an eternal operating cost. Quote lands seven figures plus O&M. You end up reissuing the renders anyway, later and more expensively.

decisionPoints.debrief: The lakes are groundwater windows: their level IS the water table, and near this coast the water is brackish. The CM's value is catching physics-vs-marketing conflicts at design review, before promises are printed. Whoever catches it latest pays the most.
